summary: This informational memo gives an overview of low-power wide-area network technologies being considered by the IETF. These wireless technologies offer wide coverage, low bandwidth, very small packets and long battery life. It describes their characteristics so protocol work can be informed.

plainLanguage.summary: Some tiny gadgets need to talk across a whole town using almost no power. This describes the radio systems built for those whispering gadgets.

questions: what are low power wide area networks
why does ipv6 not fit lpwan
subtitle: A survey of the radio technologies built to let tiny battery devices reach across kilometers, and why plain IPv6 does not fit them.

tldr.problem: Low-power wide-area radios give years of battery life and multi-kilometer range but only tiny frames, very low bit rates and tight duty cycles, and at the time of writing essentially no such end devices (other than Wi-SUN) had IP capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys four technologies (LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Sigfox and Wi-SUN FAN), sets out common terminology for their parts, and analyses where existing IETF protocols such as IPv6, 6LoWPAN, CoAP and DNS fall short.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational background document for the IPv6 over LPWAN working group, not a specification; its gap analysis lists what would need adapting to run IP on these networks.

today: RFC 8376 is an Informational RFC from May 2018, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the technologies as they stood at the time of writing and is background material, not a standard.

sections.title: What LPWANs Are and Their Shared Vocabulary
sections.content:
This memo gives background on the technologies considered in the IETF's IPv6 over Low Power Wide-Area Networks (LPWAN) working group, plus a gap analysis against current IETF specifications. Most of these technologies aim to support large numbers of very low-cost, low-throughput devices with very low power consumption, so battery-powered devices can be deployed for years. Spectrum is limited by duty cycles, usually a percentage of time per hour that a device may transmit.

LPWANs prioritize power and cost by accepting severe bandwidth and duty cycle limits, in exchange for the multiple-kilometer links implied by "Wide Area". The RFC states that its technology text was mainly contributed by proponents of each technology, is not normative, and does not weigh pros and cons.

Because the technologies use different names for similar parts, the RFC defines generic terms: end devices, the Radio Gateway, the Network Gateway, an LPWAN-AAA server that controls authentication, and the Application Server.
sections.plainLanguage: All these systems share one trick: send very little, very rarely, to save the battery. Because each one calls the parts by different names, the paper picks common names.

sections.title: LoRaWAN
sections.content:
The RFC bases its LoRaWAN description on version 1.0.2 of the LoRa Alliance specification. LoRaWAN aims for devices on a single battery for an extended period (e.g., 10 years or more) and extended coverage through 155 dB maximum coupling loss. It uses a star-of-stars topology: end devices talk single-hop over radio to one or more Gateways, which relay to a central Network Server over IP.

After each transmission, a Class A device opens two short receive windows. Default delays in the EU 868 MHz band are 1 s and 2 s (the second must be the first plus 1 s). The smallest frame size listed is 19 octets, of which 8 octets are MAC headers, leaving 11 octets for payload. The Join-Request message is 23 bytes.

Devices need a 32-bit device address and two 128-bit session keys: NwkSKey for integrity and AppSKey for confidentiality. Alternatively, a device can use the join procedure with a long-term, device-specific AppKey. All payloads are encrypted and integrity-protected, and every MAC-layer message has a 32-bit MIC calculated with AES-CMAC. MAC commands sent as frame options (FOpts) travel in clear but cannot be modified by an active attacker because of the MIC.
sections.plainLanguage: Little gadgets shout to a nearby tower, and the tower passes the message on to a boss computer. After shouting, a gadget listens for a reply for only two short moments, then goes back to sleep.

sections.title: NB-IoT
sections.content:
Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) was developed and standardized by 3GPP, with standardization finalized in 3GPP Release 13 in June 2016. It can be deployed in existing LTE networks with a software upgrade in the operator's base stations. Targets include module cost below US $5, 164 dB maximum coupling loss, battery life of over 10 years, about 55000 devices per cell, and uplink reporting latency of less than 10 seconds.

It runs half duplex FDD with a 60 kbit/s uplink peak and 30 kbit/s downlink peak, a 1600-byte MTU limited by the PDCP layer, and 180 kHz narrowbands. It can be deployed in-band, in an LTE guard band, or standalone, all in licensed spectrum, so there is no channel access restriction and up to a 100% duty cycle.

To save signalling and battery, NB-IoT adds Data-over-NAS (a mandatory control plane optimization that sends data directly to and from the MME, bypassing the Access Stratum) and optional RRC Suspend/Resume. Power-Saving Mode and extended DRX let devices sleep deeply.
sections.plainLanguage: This one uses the phone company's own towers on spectrum the company owns. Gadgets sleep most of the time and wake up just to report.

sections.title: Sigfox and Wi-SUN FAN
sections.content:
Sigfox devices send only a few bytes per day, week or month, in principle allowing 10-15 years on a battery. The radio uses Ultra Narrow Band (UNB). The uplink frame has a 19-bit preamble, 29 bits of frame sync and header, a 32-bit device ID, a payload of 0-96 bits, 16-40 bits of authentication and a 16-bit frame check sequence. Under the strictest regulations the system allows a maximum of 140 uplink and 4 downlink messages per device per day. Each message is authenticated with a device ID and an AES-128-based message authentication code, and the RFC notes the algorithm and keying details were not published at the time of writing.

Wi-SUN FAN is different: an IPv6 wireless frequency-hopping mesh. The RFC reports a range of typically 2 - 3 km line of sight and data rates up to 300 kbit/s. Nodes are Border Routers, Routers or Leaf nodes. Its stack uses UDP or TCP over IPv6 with 6LoWPAN adaptation, RPL routing, and IEEE 802.15.4-based MAC and PHY, with 802.1X and EAP-TLS for authentication. Wi-SUN is the one technology the RFC notes as already having IP capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Sigfox sends tiny, rare notes and can barely listen back. Wi-SUN is more like a neighbourhood web of relays that already speaks internet.

sections.title: Gap Analysis for IP over LPWAN
sections.content:
IPv6 has a header overhead of at least 40 bytes and requires the layer below to support at least 1280-byte packets, so naive IPv6 over an LPWAN could need several frames just for the IP header. Neighbor Discovery, DHCPv6, IPsec and TLS also need relatively frequent round trips and bulky messages.

The 6LoWPAN suite helps but is stretched by LPWAN limits: L2 payloads of roughly 10 to 100 bytes and bit rates from about 10 bit/s to 100 kbit/s. Its header compression can shrink an IPv6 header to 2 or 3 bytes in the best cases, but practical minima are 11 or 19 bytes. Its fragmentation header is costly for such small frames, and 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery may take hours or even days in the most constrained setups.

The RFC also looks at 6lo, 6tisch, RoHC, ROLL, CoAP, mobility and DNS. A DNS query-then-use pattern is called clearly problematic where only one round trip per hour is possible, and it is unclear how DNS-like functionality might work in LPWANs.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary internet messages carry a big address label, and the gadget can only send a tiny note. So tricks are needed to shrink the labels and to avoid chatty back-and-forth.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Most LPWAN technologies include authentication or encryption mechanisms defined outside the IETF. The working group may need to integrate them to unify management, and a standardized AAA infrastructure may offer a scalable solution.

Privacy is a concern: a home sensor that emits an encrypted packet every time someone enters a room makes that traffic privacy sensitive, and the RFC says it is not clear whether workable mitigations exist, since padding and cover traffic may not be feasible. Key management and certificate revocation checking, such as OCSP stapling, face the problem that certificates and OCSP responses are bulky for bandwidth-bounded LPWANs. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a scrambled message can give away things, like when somebody walks into a room. And the usual lock-and-key paperwork is too heavy for such tiny messengers.
